title: How to Design Around Cognitive Offloading
author: Dr. Philippa Hardman
summary: Hardman synthesizes a cluster of 2026 studies on cognitive offloading to move the AI-and-learning debate past a binary ban-it-or-embrace-it framing. Drawing on research from Cui et al., Ates, Wang and Zhang, Strömberg, and Dai and Chan, she argues offloading is not triggered by AI use itself but by who retains decision authority over the thinking, and that the effect is often invisible on immediate performance metrics while showing up clearly on delayed, AI-free tests. She distills the findings into six design principles for structuring learning experiences that use AI to extend rather than replace cognition, centered on the idea that the learner must judge first, delegate labor rather than judgment, and be tested with the AI switched off. The piece is aimed at instructional/learning designers building AI-integrated courses, translating research findings directly into buildable design rules rather than abstract caution.
points: Offloading tracks the incentive structure, not the tool: Cui et al. found 64.6% of AI use collapsed into replacement mode under deadline/grade pressure versus just 5.3% when students explored out of genuine interest.

The single most validated intervention is sequencing: having students self-judge their own draft for two minutes before AI feedback appears preserved long-term learning gains that instant AI feedback erased on a delayed, AI-free test (Ates, 2026).

Performance-with-AI-on is a misleading proxy for capability: the feedback design that scored best on live drafts scored worst weeks later once the AI was removed, meaning dashboards can mistake offloading for improvement.

Only 7.5% of AI conversations in the Cui dataset showed the full 'collaborator stance' (proposing, pushing back, judging AI output) — Hardman argues this stance cannot be left to learner discipline and must be designed into the task.

Delegating labor (summarizing, formatting, organizing) can deepen learning when the freed time is reinvested in judgment tasks AI can't do, but delegating the judgment itself is what destroys learning — 'the same word describing two opposite acts.'
quotes: When students used AI as a replacement for their own thinking — paste the assignment in, take what comes out — the two highest forms of thinking (judging the quality of ideas, and building on them) appeared exactly zero times.
The reason: when the AI judges first, learners stop judging their own work and simply edit the AI’s opinion. The evaluating — the part that builds the skill — had been handed over (Ates, 2026).

Students who dabbled with AI — fix a sentence here, check a fact there — learned less than students who used no AI at all. Dabblers carried all of the mental workload themselves, plus the extra effort of managing the tool, and freed up no capacity for deeper thinking.

The winning design added one small step: before the AI’s feedback opened, students spent two minutes judging their own draft — strongest point, weakest point, one thing they were unsure about, top revision priority.

On that delayed test, the AI-based designs finished both last and first, with human-only feedback in the middle. Same tool, same model, same prompts. So is AI feedback better than human feedback turns out to be the wrong question.

Students who handed entire categories of supporting work to AI — summarising sources, first-pass literature reviews, organising data — and then spent the freed time on what AI can't do for them showed the deepest learning in the study.
AI can support and enhance human cognition when — and only when — the human retains cognitive ownership. Each study conducted so far has located that ownership at three different levels of design.
Ownership has to be designed into the task and reinforced through practice — made the path of least resistance, not an act of learner virtue.
